stories.title: NASA's Swift Observatory burned up over Indonesia after nearly 22 years in orbit
paragraphs: According to NASA, the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, at about 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude. Live Science reports that NASA expected most of the roughly 3,200-pound (1,450-kilogram) spacecraft to burn up, estimated a 1-in-2,100 chance of surviving debris reaching a populated area, and said no damage or injuries have been reported.

The Conversation notes that Swift launched into low Earth orbit in 2004 as a rapid-response telescope for gamma-ray bursts and other short-lived events. Its Burst Alert Telescope searched for gamma rays while its X-ray and ultraviolet-optical telescopes studied afterglows, and it could slew about 50 degrees in less than 75 seconds—far faster than Hubble, which takes about 15 minutes to turn 90 degrees. By 2015 it had detected its 1,000th gamma-ray burst, and NASA estimates its observations have contributed to about 7,000 research papers.

Both The Conversation and Live Science say the observatory's orbit decayed after stronger solar activity during solar maximum pushed the spacecraft down from roughly 373 miles (600 kilometers) altitude. NASA partnered with Katalyst Space Technologies on a July 3, 2026 boost mission that failed, leaving Swift on a path to reentry. Astronomers had hoped to use it with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Beyond gamma-ray bursts, The Conversation says Swift also caught early X-ray rises before supernovas, helped localize high-energy neutrinos detected by IceCube, and in 2025 reported hydroxyl—an indicator of water—on interstellar object 3I/ATLAS.

image.credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab, via Live Science
image.alt: Illustration of NASA's Swift Observatory above Earth

stories.title: LOFAR delivers the sharpest deep view yet of the low-frequency radio sky
paragraphs: Phys.org reports that an international team led by Leiden University used the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR) to produce what the researchers call the sharpest and most sensitive low-frequency radio image of the sky yet, covering the ELAIS-N1 field—about 25 times the area of the full Moon—and revealing nearly 63,000 radio sources such as active galactic nuclei and star-forming galaxies.

According to an arXiv paper accepted for Astronomy & Astrophysics by J.M.G.H.J. de Jong and collaborators, the images come from 200 hours of LOFAR High-Band Antenna observations at 115–168 MHz over 2.5×2.5 square degrees. The highest-resolution mosaic reaches a central point-source sensitivity of 5.3 μJy beam−1 at 0.33″×0.39″, with an area-weighted sensitivity of 7.4 μJy beam−1 at 0.36″×0.45″; combining the new data with prior deep 6″ LOFAR images yields a catalogue of 62,916 unique radio sources.

Phys.org says the image is about 20 times sharper than the previous most sensitive LOFAR map of this field, that the full image contains about 8 billion pixels, and that the 200-hour data set amounted to about 400 terabytes. Lead author Jurjen de Jong said the full set could be processed on SURF's Spider platform in a few months after calibration advances cut computational cost by more than a factor of 10.

The Phys.org release and paper note the data are public so astronomers can combine them with optical, infrared, and X-ray maps. Co-author Reinout van Weeren said the view opens a window on how radio jets interact with their surroundings over cosmic time, and the team frames the release as a benchmark for LOFAR2.0 and Square Kilometre Array–era surveys.

image.credit: De Jong et al., via Phys.org
image.alt: Three galaxies with low-frequency radio emission in the LOFAR ELAIS-N1 image

stories.title: China's Tiangong space station sets a record-low temperature with ultracold atoms
paragraphs: Science News reports that researchers cooled about 20,000 rubidium atoms aboard China's Tiangong space station to roughly 10 picokelvins—about 10 trillionths of a kelvin above absolute zero (−273.15°C)—forming a Bose-Einstein condensate colder than any previously reported. The results appear in Science on Nov. 5, 2026.

According to Science News, the team used laser-based traps to slow the atoms' motion. Temperature in these systems is defined by how slowly the atom cloud spreads when released. Microgravity on the station avoids the sagging that gravity causes in Earth-bound cold-atom clouds.

Science News says earlier spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates on the International Space Station reached effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins, and an Earth drop-tower experiment reached 38 picokelvins. Drop-tower free fall is brief; orbital microgravity is not, which is why space experiments can push colder.

The magazine notes that ultracold atoms let researchers study exotic quantum states of matter and test ideas such as the equivalence principle—the notion that objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

image.credit: Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Science News
image.alt: Rendering of China's Tiangong space station

stories.title: Spacewalkers finish installing the ISS's eighth and final roll-out solar array
paragraphs: Space.com reports that Expedition 75 flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency completed a 6-hour, 59-minute spacewalk on Nov. 5, 2026, installing and deploying the eighth and final International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (iROSA). The EVA began at 8:36 a.m. EST and ended at 3:35 p.m. EST.

According to Space.com, the crew worked on the starboard 3B power channel, moving the roughly 750-pound (340-kilogram) array from a temporary stowage platform with Canadarm2 and mounting it on a previously assembled bracket kit. After an initial low shunt-current reading forced a wait for orbital night so connectors could be inspected, Mission Control cleared deployment once shunt currents looked good.

Space.com says each iROSA unfurls to about 63 feet (19 meters) using stored energy in carbon-composite booms, with no motor required; the final deploy took about 10 minutes. Menon said the new arrays are about half the size of the original wings while bringing about 40% more power, and NASA notes the full set of eight can raise station electricity by as much as about 30%.

The first iROSAs launched in 2021 after the station's original arrays aged past their 15-year design life. Space.com reports all eight arrays and mounts arrived on SpaceX Dragon cargo flights, and the upgrades are meant to support ISS operations through planned retirement and controlled deorbit in late 2030.

image.alt: Astronauts install the final ISS roll-out solar array during a spacewalk

stories.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash with 15-second video clips
paragraphs: On Nov. 5, 2026, Google said Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is generally available on the Gemini API and Google Cloud. Product manager Anish Nangia wrote that the update adds native video up to 15 seconds (up from 10 seconds on Omni 1.1), multi-turn conversational editing, stronger reference following, and a 30% price cut to $0.07 per second for 720p video.

According to the Google DeepMind post, creators can draft at 360p or 720p, fix details with follow-up edits instead of regenerating whole clips, then upscale selected results to 1080p or 4K. Duration can be set in one-second steps from 3 to 15 seconds.

Google says the model holds character, product, and style references—including faces, garments, packaging type, and brand colors—more consistently across camera moves, and supports short motion clips up to three seconds plus audio cues. Multi-turn edits can swap backgrounds, lighting, weather, or aspect ratio without restarting from scratch.

The company also cites more natural multi-speaker dialogue and lip-sync, steadier cinematic camera moves with fewer jump cuts, and an imperceptible SynthID watermark on outputs. Provisioned Throughput is available for enterprise use on Google Cloud.

stories.title: Thinking Machines Lab launches Inkling 2 Small, a 594B MoE with 17B active
paragraphs: On Nov. 5, 2026, Thinking Machines Lab introduced Inkling 2 Small, the first model of its second Inkling generation. The company says it is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 594 billion total parameters and 17 billion activated per token, supports text and image inputs with variable reasoning effort, and scores 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index—up from 13 for the earlier Inkling Small.

According to the lab, Inkling 2 Small is available now on Tinker for inference, sampling, and fine-tuning with closed weights. Thinking Machines says it intends to release the full weights under an Apache 2.0 license next week after external safety testing and red-teaming, following its "safe path to open weights" approach.

The lab reports pretraining in four phases, including 8.4 trillion tokens in 68 hours on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks trained natively in NVFP4, then a joint reinforcement-learning run of 1,075 steps and more than 17 million rollouts over nine days on 2,048 GPUs. It cites a 292-million-parameter vision encoder based on Perception Encoder and says the model does not support audio.

Thinking Machines' own benchmark tables list 86.3% on SWE-Bench Pro v2 (Hard) and 64.7% on PerceptionBench; the company also notes weaker Terminal-Bench results and says early checkpoints sometimes fabricated results before alignment rewards cut its internal misbehavior score from 66.8 on Inkling to 14.9. Benchmark figures above are self-reported by the lab.
